title: The Manual
author: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian)
openingText: Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions. Things not in our control are body, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions.
about:
The Manual — Encheiridion in Greek, "handbook" — is a short Stoic guide compiled around 125 CE from the lectures of Epictetus by his student Arrian. Epictetus had been born a slave in Phrygia and was lame, possibly from beatings; he became one of the most influential philosophers of the late Roman world. The Manual distills his teaching into a few dozen short chapters, designed for daily reading.

The book is meant to be carried — its name suggests something held in the hand, ready when needed. It is the most condensed expression of Stoic ethics: focus on what is in your control, accept what is not, judge events by your responses to them rather than by the events themselves. Marcus Aurelius's Meditations are unimaginable without Epictetus.

angleCards.title: The dichotomy of control.
angleCards.text: Epictetus's whole system rests on a single distinction: what is up to us and what is not. I want to work through each chapter testing whether that distinction is real — whether it actually holds under pressure, or whether it is a consoling simplification.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test the dichotomy of control — what is actually within my power and what is not — and whether it holds up as a true description of human experience.

angleCards.title: A slave writing about freedom.
angleCards.text: Epictetus was owned. He lost his external freedom completely, and that is precisely the context in which he developed a philosophy of inner freedom. I want to read the text with that biography in mind and see whether it adds weight or complicates his claims.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Epictetus as a former slave writing about freedom — and I want to understand what that context does to his philosophy, whether it makes it more or less credible.

angleCards.title: Reading it as practice.
angleCards.text: Epictetus didn't write for theorists — he wrote for people who wanted to change how they live. The Enchiridion is meant to be worked, not just read. I want to treat each chapter as an exercise and notice what actually shifts when I try to apply it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Enchiridion as a practice, not a text — working through the exercises as Epictetus intended, not just understanding the arguments intellectually.

angleCards.title: The Stoic theory of emotion.
angleCards.text: Stoics didn't say don't feel — they said don't be ruled by feelings that rest on false judgments. I want to follow their emotional theory carefully, understand what they actually claimed, and decide whether modern psychology has proved them right or wrong.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the Stoic theory of emotion — why they thought passion clouded judgment, whether they were right, and what the alternative looks like in practice.

cast.name: Epictetus
cast.description: Born a slave in Hierapolis, he became one of the most influential moral philosophers in Western history. His lectures were never written down by him — everything we have comes through his student Arrian.

cast.name: Arrian
cast.description: A Greek historian and student of Epictetus who transcribed the lectures that became the Discourses, then distilled the most essential passages into the Enchiridion — the handbook you are reading.

cast.name: The Dichotomy
cast.description: The division between what is in our power (opinion, desire, aversion, action) and what is not (body, reputation, external events). Every other teaching in the manual follows from getting this distinction right.

cast.name: The Hegemonikon
cast.description: The Stoic term for the governing part of the soul — the faculty of judgment and assent. What Epictetus means when he talks about "you": not your body or your reputation, but the thing that decides how to interpret events.

cast.name: Marcus Aurelius
cast.description: Roman emperor and Stoic practitioner whose Meditations are essentially private notes applying Epictetus's teaching. He is the most famous reader of this text, and proof that the philosophy can be lived in extreme conditions.

cast.name: Zeno of Citium
cast.description: The philosopher who founded the Stoic school in Athens around 300 BCE. Epictetus is his heir three centuries later — adapting the tradition, sharpening it, and giving it the personal urgency that makes it still readable today.

whyItMatters.title: A Practical Stoicism
whyItMatters.body: Where most philosophy is theoretical, the Manual is operational. It tells you what to do when you are angry, when you have lost something, when you are afraid. The aphoristic format is designed for daily reference, not for systematic reading.

whyItMatters.title: What Is in Your Control
whyItMatters.body: The book opens with the most important Stoic distinction: some things are in our control, others are not. The first sentence and the rest of the book are an argument that mistaking one for the other is the source of most suffering. The principle has shaped not just Stoicism but cognitive behavioral therapy and large parts of modern self-help.

whyItMatters.title: A Slave's Philosophy
whyItMatters.body: Epictetus had been a slave. He knew, more concretely than any Stoic before him, what the loss of external control feels like — and what control of the inner life looks like for someone who has none of the outer kind. The book is the most extreme test case for Stoic philosophy: does it work when external freedom is genuinely absent?
